title: Jesus prays (CCC 2598–2606)
hook: he prays at every big moment of his life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Old Testament prayer: Abraham listening, Moses pleading, David singing, Elijah waiting. Your line was the long school. Which of the four came easiest? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

Before a big choice, out comes the list. Pros, cons. A call to a friend, a night to sleep on it, other people's opinions scrolled at midnight. Luke's Gospel tells about the night before Jesus chose the twelve apostles, the men who would carry on his work. He didn't make a list. He went up a mountain to pray. And in the Douay-Rheims, "he passed the whole night in the prayer of God." When day came, he chose twelve. Today: Jesus prays.
screen: `PROS, CONS, MIDNIGHT.` → `UP A MOUNTAIN TO PRAY.` → `THE WHOLE NIGHT IN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The Catechism points out that Luke's Gospel keeps showing Jesus praying at the turning points. At his baptism in the Jordan, while he prays, the heavens open. Before choosing the Twelve, a whole night. Before Peter says who Jesus is, he has been praying alone. On the mountain of the Transfiguration, his face changes as he prays. And the Catechism adds a quieter habit: he often slipped away to lonely places, sometimes at night, to pray. Then the Catechism notices something tender about where he learned. It says that, as a boy, Jesus learned to pray with his human heart from his mother, and in the synagogue and the Temple, with the words and rhythms of his people. And yet his prayer comes from somewhere deeper: from his relationship with the Father. Listen to how his prayers begin. At the tomb of Lazarus, before he calls his friend out, he says, "Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me." Thanks, before the miracle. Then the garden, the night before he dies. In Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "not my will, but thine be done." The Catechism says the garden gives a glimpse of the depth of his prayer as Son: trust, and a will handed over. Mark keeps the Aramaic word he used: Abba, Father. Even on the cross, he prays. He prays for the ones crucifying him, and at the end he commends his spirit into his Father's hands. So in the Catechism's picture, Jesus is not only the one Christians pray to. He's the one who prayed first, and taught by doing it.
screen: `LUKE: PRAYER AT THE TURNING POINTS.` · `LEARNED FROM HIS MOTHER.` · `THANKS, BEFORE THE MIRACLE.` · `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before a decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one choice in front of you, large or small. A job, a conversation, what to say yes to this week. Don't weigh it yet. Don't make the list. Just hold it, the way Jesus took the night before choosing. If you pray, you can bring it to God, and if you're ready, add the words from the garden. If you don't, just let it rest in quiet before you decide. The bell holds the time.

Jesus prays. In the Gospels, at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, on the mountain, in the garden and on the cross: in Catholic teaching, the one who prays first, and teaches by praying. Today's word.
Your line: he prayed first. Today, before one decision, however small, take a breath of quiet before you choose. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics look to Jesus as the model of prayer, and some keep his habits: prayer before decisions, time alone in quiet, thanksgiving, and the garden's handing over of the will, echoed in the Lord's Prayer's thy will be done.
